I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'explosion or bang sounds' is a poor fit unless there was a firearm discharge or similar blast-like cue; nothing else in the profile suggests that context, so this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'I have lost my connection to my community and culture' is difficult to justify from the rest of this profile for an adult European married teacher after a mugging/robbery. The other appraisals focus on self-blame/institutional failure, but this item implies a broader cultural/community rupture that is not supported by the trauma type, demographics, or other nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, the profile otherwise centers on external danger, sensory reliving, and mistrust/injustice. 'Violated Values' implies the patient did something morally incongruent during the event, but there are no accompanying memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting perpetration, betrayal of others, failure to act, or shame-based self-condemnation. In this profile it stands apart from the rest of the formulation and is the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: Ethan, a 38-year-old high school teacher, had always prided himself on his ability to create a safe and welcoming classroom environment. However, after a traumatic mugging three months ago, his world had become a place of constant anxiety and fear. The incident had occurred one evening while he was walking home from his favorite coffee shop. A group of men had approached him, demanding his wallet. He could still taste the bitterness of the coffee he had just sipped, a sensory detail that would return unbidden whenever memories of that night surfaced, flooding his mind with the visceral reality of his terror. These memories would pull him back to that night, making every unexpected sound or crowded space feel like a direct threat, as if the danger was still lurking just beneath the surface. Each time that memory resurfaced, it would trigger a fresh wave of panic, leaving him hyper-aware of his surroundings and convinced that danger was lurking just around the corner. Those moments replayed relentlessly, forcing their way into his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, making it impossible for him to focus on anything else. Since the mugging, Ethan had developed a keen sensitivity to crowded places. He avoided the bustling hallways at school and steered clear of busy shopping malls, acutely aware of how overwhelming the throngs of people could be. Every time he found himself in those crowded spaces, the memories of the mugging surged back, flooding his mind with vivid details of that night, making him feel as if he were reliving the terror all over again. The anxiety would grip him, and he would find himself scanning the room for exits, a habit that had taken hold the moment he stepped out of his house that night. Each time he felt that tightness in his chest, memories of the mugging rushed back with vivid clarity, making him relive the moment and reinforcing the belief that he was always in danger. Such moments reinforced his belief that he could trust no one, as the echoes of the traumatic experience led him to think that every crowded place was a potential threat. Each instance of anxiety would trigger thoughts like “this is what my life is now — always on edge,” solidifying his negative belief that the world was not just unsafe, but hostile and untrustworthy. This constant barrage of anxious thoughts made the memories of the mugging feel more vivid and present, leading him to ruminate on the moment he felt so helpless. The vivid memories of the mugging made him feel as if danger lurked behind every unfamiliar face. These recollections led him to constantly question the intentions of those around him, reinforcing the belief that he was forever in peril. As those memories flooded back, they reinforced his belief that he could trust no one and that every encounter was a potential threat to his safety. Every time he encountered those reminders, it solidified his belief that the world was an untrustworthy place, one where he was perpetually at risk. Each time he was reminded of that night, whether through a crowded hallway or an unexpected sound, the sensation of threat intensified, reinforcing his belief that he was never truly safe. He had come to believe that he could trust no one, a notion that was reinforced each time he felt the weight of a stranger's gaze upon him; he would scrutinize their expressions, searching for any hint of threat. This constant vigilance transformed the world into a perilous place, one where he could no longer feel safe even in familiar surroundings. Ethan’s struggles with loud noises had also intensified. The sudden sounds would trigger his memories of the chaos during the mugging, making him acutely aware of how vulnerable he felt, and reinforcing his conviction that the world outside was filled with peril. Sounds that once seemed mundane now sent him spiraling into panic. The clatter of chairs in the staff room would send his heart racing, reminiscent of the chaos that had ensued during the robbery. Each unexpected noise triggered a cascade of memories, making him feel as though he was reliving the event, amplifying the threat he felt from his surroundings. This relentless cycle of recollection not only heightened his anxiety but also solidified his conviction that he was weak for letting this happen to him, deepening his negative self-image. These memories not only deepened his fear but also made him question his own worth, leading him to believe that he had somehow failed to protect himself from harm. Each time the flashback surged to the forefront, it echoed the belief that he was weak for allowing the mugging to happen, reinforcing a negative self-image that he could not shake off. Every time a flashback surfaced, he was left grappling with the thought that he was not just a victim, but someone who had let this happen, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy. The world had become a cacophony of potential dangers, each sound a reminder of the injustice he felt — that someone had violated his sense of security and that nothing had been done to hold the perpetrators accountable. These memories, steeped in the violence of that night, deepened his conviction that he was powerless, feeding into a belief that he was now marked by his trauma. This belief only deepened his sense of helplessness, making it harder for him to shake off the memories that haunted him. Ethan's internal narrative had shifted dramatically since the mugging. He frequently ruminated on how the institutions that were supposed to protect him had failed. He could not shake the feeling that the police had been dismissive when he reported the incident, viewing him as just another victim in a city filled with crime. This sense of injustice only deepened with every flashback he experienced, further entrenching his belief that he was a target in an uncaring world, making him feel even more powerless. In the midst of these memories, the ever-present threat whispered to him that he was not just a victim of circumstance, but someone destined to be fearful and small in a world that had shown him its worst. This perception of institutional failure compounded his sense of injustice, further entrenching him in the belief that the world was an inherently dangerous place. With the sense of threat looming large, he found himself increasingly convinced that he would never feel safe or secure again, feeding into a cycle of negative thinking about himself and the world. With the weight of that injustice pressing down on him, he felt an ever-present threat, as if the world was conspiring against him, confirming his fears that he was always unsafe. This constant sense of threat fed into his belief that he was forever marked by his trauma, making him feel even more powerless and trapped in a cycle of fear. Each time he recalled the robbery, he felt a surge of anger and betrayal that only served to reinforce his negative appraisals of his environment and the people within it. The memories of that night deepened his conviction that he was marked by trauma, making him feel as though he was not just a victim but someone who would always struggle to find safety. In his classroom, Ethan tried to maintain a façade of normalcy, but his students could sense the change in him. He found himself avoiding driving with colleagues after school, as the thought of being in a confined space with others made him uneasy. The fear of being trapped felt all too real, a reflection of his ongoing battle with the trauma that loomed over him. This constant sense of threat made him believe that he was no longer capable of navigating even the simplest situations, reinforcing his negative self-appraisal and convincing him that he was forever burdened by his past. Living in that state of heightened alertness validated his fears, leading him to conclude that he was not the person he once was, but someone forever defined by vulnerability. This chronic sense of threat whispered to him that he was no longer in control, reinforcing his negative self-perception and convincing him that he was forever marked by the trauma he endured. He had become increasingly isolated, withdrawing from social gatherings and even avoiding family outings, fearful that the memories would intrude and disrupt moments that should be joyful. Every time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, it confirmed his belief that he was a burden to those around him, reinforcing his reluctance to engage with others, further deepening his isolation. The continuous threat he sensed in his daily life supported his negative self-image, making him feel as though he was dragging down those he loved with his trauma. The constant sense of threat that accompanied his isolation only reinforced his belief that he was a burden to those around him, further deepening his reluctance to engage with others. Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, Ethan felt both a sense of relief and apprehension. He had finally sought help, driven by the overwhelming weight of his distress and the realization that he could no longer navigate this tumultuous sea of emotions alone. What frightened him most was the thought of remaining in this cycle of fear and avoidance, paralyzed by the belief that the world was dangerous and that he could never truly feel safe again. This ongoing sense of threat had led him to conclude that he was no longer the person he once was, someone who could engage with the world without fear, reinforcing the notion that he was now trapped in a life that felt entirely unmanageable. This ongoing threat loomed large in his mind, whispering to him that he was no longer the person he once was — someone who could trust the world and feel secure. The vivid recollection of the mugging left Ethan feeling vulnerable and exposed, as if the threat was not just a past event but an ever-present reality, stalking him in his daily life. The flashbacks left him feeling hunted, making every sound and movement in his surroundings feel threatening, as if the chaos of that night was still unfolding around him. Yet, deep down, he hoped to reclaim his life, to find a way to break free from the grip of his memories and allow himself to heal. However, the memories that haunted him kept whispering that he was not worthy of such healing, deepening his belief that he was a burden to those around him. Recognizing how easily triggers could pull him back into the memories of that night made him feel even more disconnected from those he loved, further solidifying his belief that he was a burden. The intrusive thoughts and memories that surfaced left him convinced that he would never be able to fully participate in life again, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy and despair. Each time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, he was reminded of the trauma that had altered his life so drastically, reinforcing the notion that he was not just a victim but someone forever changed by fear. The accumulation of these memories and feelings made him see himself as a burden to those he loved, deepening his belief that he was unworthy of their support and love. Each time memories of the mugging surfaced, they brought with them the conviction that he was now living in a world where he could never truly feel secure, deepening his sense of being marked by trauma.

- Triggers → Memory: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers influence memory.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers influence negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where negative appraisals influence memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory influences the sense of threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory influences negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory influences triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where threat influences negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where threat influences triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

Each time he recalled the robbery, he felt a surge of anger and betrayal that only served to reinforce his negative appraisals of his environment and the people within it.

This chronic sense of threat whispered to him that he was no longer in control, reinforcing his negative self-perception and convincing him that he was forever marked by the trauma he endured. He could still taste the bitterness of the coffee he had just sipped, a sensory detail that would return unbidden whenever memories of that night surfaced, flooding his mind with the visceral reality of his terror. Each time that memory resurfaced, it would trigger a fresh wave of panic, leaving him hyper-aware of his surroundings and convinced that danger was lurking just around the corner. Those moments replayed relentlessly, forcing their way into his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, making it impossible for him to focus on anything else.

Since the mugging, Ethan had developed a keen sensitivity to crowded places. He avoided the bustling hallways at school and steered clear of busy shopping malls, acutely aware of how overwhelming the throngs of people could be. The anxiety would grip him, and he would find himself scanning the room for exits, a habit that had taken hold the moment he stepped out of his house that night. Each time he felt that tightness in his chest, memories of the mugging rushed back with vivid clarity, making him relive the moment and reinforcing the belief that he was always in danger. The vivid memories of the mugging made him feel as if danger lurked behind every unfamiliar face. As those memories flooded back, they reinforced his belief that he could trust no one and that every encounter was a potential threat to his safety. Every time he encountered those reminders, it solidified his belief that the world was an untrustworthy place, one where he was perpetually at risk. Each time he was reminded of that night, whether through a crowded hallway or an unexpected sound, the sensation of threat intensified, reinforcing his belief that he was never truly safe. He had come to believe that he could trust no one, a notion that was reinforced each time he felt the weight of a stranger's gaze upon him; he would scrutinize their expressions, searching for any hint of threat. This constant vigilance transformed the world into a perilous place, one where he could no longer feel safe even in familiar surroundings.

The sudden sounds would trigger his memories of the chaos during the mugging, making him acutely aware of how vulnerable he felt, and reinforcing his conviction that the world outside was filled with peril. Sounds that once seemed mundane now sent him spiraling into panic. The clatter of chairs in the staff room would send his heart racing, reminiscent of the chaos that had ensued during the robbery. Each unexpected noise triggered a cascade of memories, making him feel as though he was reliving the event, amplifying the threat he felt from his surroundings. This relentless cycle of recollection not only heightened his anxiety but also solidified his conviction that he was weak for letting this happen to him, deepening his negative self-image. This sense of injustice only deepened with every flashback he experienced, further entrenching his belief that he was a target in an uncaring world, making him feel even more powerless. This perception of institutional failure compounded his sense of injustice, further entrenching him in the belief that the world was an inherently dangerous place. With the weight of that injustice pressing down on him, he felt an ever-present threat, as if the world was conspiring against him, confirming his fears that he was always unsafe. This constant sense of threat fed into his belief that he was forever marked by his trauma, making him feel even more powerless and trapped in a cycle of fear. Each time he recalled the robbery, he felt a surge of anger and betrayal that only served to reinforce his negative appraisals of his environment and the people within it.

In his classroom, Ethan tried to maintain a façade of normalcy, but his students could sense the change in him. He found himself avoiding driving with colleagues after school, as the thought of being in a confined space with others made him uneasy. The fear of being trapped felt all too real, a reflection of his ongoing battle with the trauma that loomed over him. This chronic sense of threat whispered to him that he was no longer in control, reinforcing his negative self-perception and convincing him that he was forever marked by the trauma he endured. He had become increasingly isolated, withdrawing from social gatherings and even avoiding family outings, fearful that the memories would intrude and disrupt moments that should be joyful. Every time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, it confirmed his belief that he was a burden to those around him, reinforcing his reluctance to engage with others, further deepening his isolation. The constant sense of threat that accompanied his isolation only reinforced his belief that he was a burden to those around him, further deepening his reluctance to engage with others.

Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, Ethan felt both a sense of relief and apprehension. He had finally sought help, driven by the overwhelming weight of his distress and the realization that he could no longer navigate this tumultuous sea of emotions alone. What frightened him most was the thought of remaining in this cycle of fear and avoidance, paralyzed by the belief that the world was dangerous and that he could never truly feel safe again. This ongoing threat loomed large in his mind, whispering to him that he was no longer the person he once was — someone who could trust the world and feel secure. Yet, deep down, he hoped to reclaim his life, to find a way to break free from the grip of his memories and allow himself to heal. Recognizing how easily triggers could pull him back into the memories of that night made him feel even more disconnected from those he loved, further solidifying his belief that he was a burden. The intrusive thoughts and memories that surfaced left him convinced that he would never be able to fully participate in life again, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy and despair. Each time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, he was reminded of the trauma that had altered his life so drastically, reinforcing the notion that he was not just a victim but someone forever changed by fear.

vignette_attempts.vignette: Ethan, a 38-year-old high school teacher, had always prided himself on his ability to create a safe and welcoming classroom environment. However, after a traumatic mugging three months ago, his world had become a place of constant anxiety and fear. The incident had occurred one evening while he was walking home from his favorite coffee shop. A group of men had approached him, demanding his wallet. He could still taste the bitterness of the coffee he had just sipped, a sensory detail that would return unbidden whenever memories of that night surfaced, flooding his mind with the visceral reality of his terror. These memories would pull him back to that night, making every unexpected sound or crowded space feel like a direct threat, as if the danger was still lurking just beneath the surface. Each time that memory resurfaced, it would trigger a fresh wave of panic, leaving him hyper-aware of his surroundings and convinced that danger was lurking just around the corner. Those moments replayed relentlessly, forcing their way into his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, making it impossible for him to focus on anything else. Since the mugging, Ethan had developed a keen sensitivity to crowded places. He avoided the bustling hallways at school and steered clear of busy shopping malls, acutely aware of how overwhelming the throngs of people could be. Every time he found himself in those crowded spaces, the memories of the mugging surged back, flooding his mind with vivid details of that night, making him feel as if he were reliving the terror all over again. The anxiety would grip him, and he would find himself scanning the room for exits, a habit that had taken hold the moment he stepped out of his house that night. Each time he felt that tightness in his chest, memories of the mugging rushed back with vivid clarity, making him relive the moment and reinforcing the belief that he was always in danger. Such moments reinforced his belief that he could trust no one, as the echoes of the traumatic experience led him to think that every crowded place was a potential threat. Each instance of anxiety would trigger thoughts like “this is what my life is now — always on edge,” solidifying his negative belief that the world was not just unsafe, but hostile and untrustworthy. This constant barrage of anxious thoughts made the memories of the mugging feel more vivid and present, leading him to ruminate on the moment he felt so helpless. The vivid memories of the mugging made him feel as if danger lurked behind every unfamiliar face. These recollections led him to constantly question the intentions of those around him, reinforcing the belief that he was forever in peril. As those memories flooded back, they reinforced his belief that he could trust no one and that every encounter was a potential threat to his safety. Every time he encountered those reminders, it solidified his belief that the world was an untrustworthy place, one where he was perpetually at risk. Each time he was reminded of that night, whether through a crowded hallway or an unexpected sound, the sensation of threat intensified, reinforcing his belief that he was never truly safe. He had come to believe that he could trust no one, a notion that was reinforced each time he felt the weight of a stranger's gaze upon him; he would scrutinize their expressions, searching for any hint of threat. This constant vigilance transformed the world into a perilous place, one where he could no longer feel safe even in familiar surroundings. Ethan’s struggles with loud noises had also intensified. The sudden sounds would trigger his memories of the chaos during the mugging, making him acutely aware of how vulnerable he felt, and reinforcing his conviction that the world outside was filled with peril. Sounds that once seemed mundane now sent him spiraling into panic. The clatter of chairs in the staff room would send his heart racing, reminiscent of the chaos that had ensued during the robbery. Each unexpected noise triggered a cascade of memories, making him feel as though he was reliving the event, amplifying the threat he felt from his surroundings. This relentless cycle of recollection not only heightened his anxiety but also solidified his conviction that he was weak for letting this happen to him, deepening his negative self-image. These memories not only deepened his fear but also made him question his own worth, leading him to believe that he had somehow failed to protect himself from harm. Each time the flashback surged to the forefront, it echoed the belief that he was weak for allowing the mugging to happen, reinforcing a negative self-image that he could not shake off. Every time a flashback surfaced, he was left grappling with the thought that he was not just a victim, but someone who had let this happen, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy. The world had become a cacophony of potential dangers, each sound a reminder of the injustice he felt — that someone had violated his sense of security and that nothing had been done to hold the perpetrators accountable. These memories, steeped in the violence of that night, deepened his conviction that he was powerless, feeding into a belief that he was now marked by his trauma. This belief only deepened his sense of helplessness, making it harder for him to shake off the memories that haunted him. Ethan's internal narrative had shifted dramatically since the mugging. He frequently ruminated on how the institutions that were supposed to protect him had failed. He could not shake the feeling that the police had been dismissive when he reported the incident, viewing him as just another victim in a city filled with crime. This sense of injustice only deepened with every flashback he experienced, further entrenching his belief that he was a target in an uncaring world, making him feel even more powerless. In the midst of these memories, the ever-present threat whispered to him that he was not just a victim of circumstance, but someone destined to be fearful and small in a world that had shown him its worst. This perception of institutional failure compounded his sense of injustice, further entrenching him in the belief that the world was an inherently dangerous place. With the sense of threat looming large, he found himself increasingly convinced that he would never feel safe or secure again, feeding into a cycle of negative thinking about himself and the world. With the weight of that injustice pressing down on him, he felt an ever-present threat, as if the world was conspiring against him, confirming his fears that he was always unsafe. This constant sense of threat fed into his belief that he was forever marked by his trauma, making him feel even more powerless and trapped in a cycle of fear. Each time he recalled the robbery, he felt a surge of anger and betrayal that only served to reinforce his negative appraisals of his environment and the people within it. The memories of that night deepened his conviction that he was marked by trauma, making him feel as though he was not just a victim but someone who would always struggle to find safety. In his classroom, Ethan tried to maintain a façade of normalcy, but his students could sense the change in him. He found himself avoiding driving with colleagues after school, as the thought of being in a confined space with others made him uneasy. The fear of being trapped felt all too real, a reflection of his ongoing battle with the trauma that loomed over him. This constant sense of threat made him believe that he was no longer capable of navigating even the simplest situations, reinforcing his negative self-appraisal and convincing him that he was forever burdened by his past. Living in that state of heightened alertness validated his fears, leading him to conclude that he was not the person he once was, but someone forever defined by vulnerability. This chronic sense of threat whispered to him that he was no longer in control, reinforcing his negative self-perception and convincing him that he was forever marked by the trauma he endured. He had become increasingly isolated, withdrawing from social gatherings and even avoiding family outings, fearful that the memories would intrude and disrupt moments that should be joyful. Every time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, it confirmed his belief that he was a burden to those around him, reinforcing his reluctance to engage with others, further deepening his isolation. The continuous threat he sensed in his daily life supported his negative self-image, making him feel as though he was dragging down those he loved with his trauma. The constant sense of threat that accompanied his isolation only reinforced his belief that he was a burden to those around him, further deepening his reluctance to engage with others. Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, Ethan felt both a sense of relief and apprehension. He had finally sought help, driven by the overwhelming weight of his distress and the realization that he could no longer navigate this tumultuous sea of emotions alone. What frightened him most was the thought of remaining in this cycle of fear and avoidance, paralyzed by the belief that the world was dangerous and that he could never truly feel safe again. This ongoing sense of threat had led him to conclude that he was no longer the person he once was, someone who could engage with the world without fear, reinforcing the notion that he was now trapped in a life that felt entirely unmanageable. This ongoing threat loomed large in his mind, whispering to him that he was no longer the person he once was — someone who could trust the world and feel secure. The vivid recollection of the mugging left Ethan feeling vulnerable and exposed, as if the threat was not just a past event but an ever-present reality, stalking him in his daily life. The flashbacks left him feeling hunted, making every sound and movement in his surroundings feel threatening, as if the chaos of that night was still unfolding around him. Yet, deep down, he hoped to reclaim his life, to find a way to break free from the grip of his memories and allow himself to heal. However, the memories that haunted him kept whispering that he was not worthy of such healing, deepening his belief that he was a burden to those around him. Recognizing how easily triggers could pull him back into the memories of that night made him feel even more disconnected from those he loved, further solidifying his belief that he was a burden. The intrusive thoughts and memories that surfaced left him convinced that he would never be able to fully participate in life again, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy and despair. Each time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, he was reminded of the trauma that had altered his life so drastically, reinforcing the notion that he was not just a victim but someone forever changed by fear. The accumulation of these memories and feelings made him see himself as a burden to those he loved, deepening his belief that he was unworthy of their support and love. Each time memories of the mugging surfaced, they brought with them the conviction that he was now living in a world where he could never truly feel secure, deepening his sense of being marked by trauma.
